A 20MW Qatar data centre has broken ground. No contractor named.
Ground breaking is the easy date. Commissioning leadership is the hard one.
 
Syntyss started building a 20MW facility, designed to meet Tier 3 requirements, on an existing Qatar campus on 12 November. Project value and completion date are not disclosed, so the hiring clock is not visible yet.

The overlooked part: project value and completion date are not disclosed, so the hiring clock is not visible yet.
  
▪ 20MW, designed to meet Tier 3 requirements 
▪ Built on an existing Syntys campus 
▪ A range of rack densities, including higher-density setups for GPU-based AI and HPC 
▪ Syntys now operates four Qatar campuses, two added through the QData QFZ acquisition earlier this year ▪ Project value and completion date: not disclosed 
▪ Contractor: not named
  
Source: MEED, 13 November 2026. The ceremony was attended by Qatar's communications minister and representatives of government and industry, per MEED.
  
My read, as an observer rather than anyone close to the project:
  
A site start with no contractor named may mean the delivery team is still forming, or simply not announced. I can't tell which.
  
If it is forming, the senior roles needed early on a Tier 3 build typically include programme and construction leadership, MEP, commercial and contracts, project controls and HSQE. Commissioning and operational readiness follow. That is a sequence, not a forecast.
  
The report notes the campus already has power and fibre. It does not say whether 20MW sits within that supply or needs further upgrade.
  
Where senior or specialist hiring is needed on data centre projects across the GCC, INYA can also support. 
  
For those closer to the project: how far ahead of site start does MEP and commissioning leadership need to be in place?

Most entrepreneurs aren’t losing to AI.
They’re losing to founders using the right AI.

Every week, I see founders burning cash and focus on "shiny object" subscriptions—while a quiet minority uses a boring, ruthless stack of 3–4 tools to run a 10-person operation solo.

The gap between AI that prints leverage and AI that creates busywork has never been wider.

After testing dozens of workflows across product building, operations, and distribution, here is the real divide right now:

🟢 WHAT IS ACTUALLY SAVING TIME & MAKING MONEY:

1. "Invisible Glue" Automation (n8n, Make, Zapier + Webhooks)
AI in isolation is a toy. AI connected to your payment links, intake forms, cloud storage, and customer onboarding is an employee. Automating the handoff between a customer paying and receiving their deliverable saves 15+ hours of manual ops a week.

2. Rapid Prototyping & "Vibe Coding" (Cursor, Claude, v0)
Founders used to spend 3 months and thousands of dollars hiring agencies just to validate an MVP or build an interactive web asset. Today, you can go from a rough sketch to a live, revenue-ready prototype over a weekend—and iterate based on real buyer feedback by Monday.

3. Deep Market & Competitor Synthesis (Perplexity, NotebookLM)
Instead of drowning in 40 open browser tabs, smart operators dump competitor teardowns, vendor contracts, and raw customer feedback into grounded research tools to extract pricing gaps and positioning angles in 10 minutes.

4. Founder-Led Content Structuring (Voice-to-Draft Workflows)
Recording a 3-minute voice note about a real client problem you solved today, then using AI to structure it into a sharp post or pitch deck. The insight is 100% human; the formatting takes 30 seconds.

🔴 WHAT IS PURE HYPE (AND ACTUALLY HURTING FOUNDERS):

1. "Set-and-Forget" Autonomous Cold Email Bots
Blasting 5,000 prospects with fake AI "personalization" doesn't build pipeline anymore. It burns your domain reputation, annoys decision-makers, and permanently cheapens your brand.

2. One-Prompt "Write My Marketing" Wrappers
If your content or sales copy starts with "In today's fast-paced digital landscape," your buyers have already scrolled past. AI cannot manufacture lived experience, taste, or customer empathy.

3. Overpriced Single-Feature Wrappers
Half the tools launching right now are a $49/month subscription wrapped around a single system prompt you could build yourself in 5 minutes.

The rule I use before adding any tool to my stack:
Does this shorten the distance between customer problem and delivered value?
If it just helps me generate more noise faster, it’s a distraction.

Which AI tool has actually earned its spot in your daily workflow—and which one did you cancel the fastest? 👇

**POST TITLE:** 
Stop Applying, Start Hunting: The "Client Hunter" Strategy for Job Seekers

**LINKEDIN POST:**

The "Apply" button is becoming a graveyard for great resumes. 

If you’re a job seeker relying solely on job boards, you’re competing with hundreds (sometimes thousands) of people for the same 20% of available roles.

The reality? Up to 80% of jobs are never publicly advertised. This is the "Hidden Job Market," and you won’t find it by scrolling—you find it by hunting.

It’s time to shift your mindset from **Passive Applicant** to **Client Hunter.**

In the freelance and contract world, we don’t wait for a "Help Wanted" sign. We look for companies with problems we can solve. Here is how you can apply the "Client Hunter" framework to your job search today:

1. **Identify the "Pain Signals"**
Don’t just look for job titles. Look for triggers. Did a company just secure Series A funding? Did they just launch a new product line? Are they expanding into a new territory? These are signals that they need talent *now*, even if a job description isn't live yet.

2. **Use AI to Your Advantage**
Tools like ClientHunter or cold outreach automation aren't just for sales teams anymore. Use them to identify decision-makers and high-growth companies. Instead of manual searching, let technology surface the leads while you focus on the strategy.

3. **Pitch the Solution, Not Your Resume**
A resume tells people what you *did*. A "Hunter" tells people what they *can do* for the company. When you reach out to a hiring manager, don't ask for a job. Point out a specific challenge they might be facing and offer a 15-minute "bridge call" to discuss how you’ve solved it before.

4. **Quality Over Volume**
Sending 100 generic applications is a recipe for burnout. Sending 10 highly researched, personalized "Hunter" emails to the right people is a recipe for an interview.

The market is crowded, but the "hidden" market is wide open for those willing to do the legwork.

Are you still waiting for the right job to be posted, or are you going out to find it?

AI: A Threat to Ordinary People or an Opportunity to Create a New Middle Class?

Artificial intelligence brings enormous risks, but also opportunities that we may not yet fully understand.
One of the biggest risks lies in the labour market. People who fail to adapt to new technologies and changing ways of working may quickly lose their economic position. There is a real danger of creating a new category of poverty – people who are not necessarily less capable or less valuable, but who simply fail to adapt to the new reality.
However, there is another side to this story that, in my opinion, does not receive enough attention.
For the first time, AI gives ordinary people access to knowledge and tools that, until recently, were largely available only to those with money, connections or access to exclusive professional networks.
Through my own experience with product development, prototyping and patents, I recently discovered just how many government support schemes, funding opportunities and financial incentives actually exist – opportunities that many people simply don't know about.
Information may be publicly available, but access to it in practice often depends on whom you know, which circles you belong to and whether you have access to people who already understand the system.
This is where AI can make an enormous difference.
Today, an individual can research their legal rights, understand contracts, identify funding opportunities, develop business ideas, analyse markets, prepare documentation and access knowledge that previously required hiring several different professionals.
Of course, AI is not infallible and cannot replace qualified experts in every field. But it can significantly lower the barriers that have traditionally kept ordinary people away from opportunities.

I therefore believe AI could create two very different futures.
On one side, a new group of people who fail to adapt and become even more economically vulnerable.
On the other, a new and stronger middle class – people who know how to use technology, solve problems independently, develop ideas and create additional economic value.
These people will be less dependent on large institutions, employers, intermediaries and closed professional networks. They will be better informed, more independent and in a stronger position to negotiate their own future.
Perhaps this is the most important social consequence of the AI revolution: the possibility of giving ordinary people greater economic and personal independence.

AI will not automatically make society fairer. But for the first time, we have a tool that could significantly reduce the advantage held by individuals and organisations simply because they control access to knowledge.

The question is no longer just who will have access to AI.
The question is who will learn to use it – and who will be left behind.

Building Alphazox has become a daily experiment in aligning ambition with the practicalities of rapid growth. When we decided to replace a monolithic data‑processing service with a set of micro‑services, the excitement was immediate—but the reality hit us in the first sprint. Our engineers discovered that the new services introduced subtle latency spikes that only appeared under real‑world load, something our test suites had never reproduced. Rather than pushing a quick fix, we opened a transparent post‑mortem channel, invited the ops team to sit with developers, and collectively rewrote the contract tests to mirror production traffic patterns. The process reminded us that speed without observability creates hidden debt. Another lesson emerged from hiring. We wanted world‑class AI talent, yet many candidates hesitated about joining a still‑young company. We responded by sharing candid snapshots of our day‑to‑day code reviews, our "bug-bounty-for-learning" sessions, and the fact that we still debug on whiteboards over coffee. The authenticity resonated, and we now have a small but diverse group who feel ownership from day one. These moments don’t make headlines, but they shape the culture we’re building—one where transparency, iterative learning, and a willingness to admit uncertainty are as valuable as any technology stack.

An hour saved needs a value attached to it. Someone has to decide what that hour was worth, whether the task was completed properly and what the team can now do with the time. A busy assistant produces plenty of activity for a dashboard. A budget conversation asks rather more of the evidence.

Francesco Signorato, CEO, Diego Fiori, CTO, and Julien Roux, CRO, built Nebuly around understanding how people use AI. The Turin- and New York-based company announced a $21M Series A on November 12, led by Planven, to take that work further into the economics of enterprise AI.

Exor Ventures, Tenacity Capital and TGVG Capital participated, as did Fastweb+Vodafone through Founders Factory, alongside returning investors and angels. CDP Venture Capital SGR also supported the round through its Artificial Intelligence Fund and Digital Transition Fund.

Nebuly connects to the agents companies already run, including custom tools and assistants built on Claude, ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot. For employee tools, its platform examines tasks, estimated time savings, AI costs and where training could improve how people work. Customer-facing analytics surface experience problems, churn signals and upsell opportunities.

The distinction matters inside the buying organization. A customer conversation can reveal commercial intent without establishing how much revenue the assistant caused. A productivity estimate can identify available capacity while leaving the manager responsible for turning it into something useful. Keeping the assumptions visible gives finance and operating teams a calculation they can argue with productively.

Nebuly reports multiple six-figure contracts and names Oura, Iveco Group, Fastweb+Vodafone, CNH and Zeiss among its customers. Its Iveco case study describes dozens of internal copilots, the sort of estate where one enthusiastic team's survey can tell a very incomplete story.

The funding will support US and European go-to-market expansion and platform development. As Nebuly reaches more enterprises, its software will enter the meeting where a saved hour gets assigned to the next job, the next customer or the next hiring plan. That is where the people using AI and the people funding it have to settle on the same version of value.

OpenAI and Upwork have published a joint study on how AI is changing freelance work. The numbers that stood out are about project size, not hourly rates.

Fixed price budgets on AI related Upwork jobs are about 52% higher than on similar non AI jobs. Posted hourly rates are only about 1.5% higher.

So clients aren’t paying much more per hour. They’re buying bigger projects. On hourly contracts, AI related work also logged around 41% more hours in the first 90 days after hiring.

The authors call it “rebundling”: clients packing more kinds of work into one project. In AI related jobs, 8.4% of task pairs were combinations clients rarely asked for together before generative AI, against 2.4% in other jobs. Think AI generated video plus editing plus motion graphics, or a chatbot plus the app it has to live inside.

Two cautions. “AI related” means the job asks for AI skills or tools, or involves improving AI output. And this is one platform’s data, describing patterns rather than proving cause.

The report also notes that graphic and presentation design, video, and web development make up a much bigger share of Upwork job posts than of ChatGPT conversations. It reads that as continued demand for people who deliver finished work.

Separate news from the same week: Upwork told the SEC it now expects to cut about 37% of its total workforce, up from 24%. That’s a company restructuring. The study doesn’t link the two.

My reading as a freelance designer: the brief seems to be moving from a single task toward a finished outcome. That’s my interpretation, not the report’s.

If you hire freelancers, are you asking for bigger bundles of work than you were two years ago?

Who Is Liable When AI Gets It Wrong?
An AI tool drafts a contract with a flawed clause. A chatbot gives a customer false information. A hiring algorithm screens out qualified candidates.
Who is responsible? The law is still catching up, but the early answer is clear: "the AI did it" is not a defense.
🔎 The three parties in the chain
1. The developer builds the model. They may face claims over defects, misleading capabilities, or biased training data.
2. The deployer is the business that puts the tool in front of customers or employees. This is where most liability lands, because you chose the tool and you control how it's used.
3. The user is the person who relies on the output. A professional who submits unchecked AI work is still accountable for it.
📌 What this means in practice
▪️ Regulators in many regions are moving toward risk-based AI rules. The higher the impact on people's rights, jobs, or money, the stricter the duties.
▪️ Contracts with AI vendors now matter more. Look at indemnity, data use, and accuracy warranties.
▪️ Courts have already sanctioned lawyers for submitting AI-generated citations that didn't exist.
✅ Your action checklist
Keep a list of every AI tool your team uses.
Require human review before any AI output reaches a client or decision.
Review vendor contracts for liability terms.
Write a short internal AI-use policy.
AI can speed up your work, but it can't take the blame for it.

I am writing a book because of one clause I never wrote in 23 years of managed services contracts. Those contracts carried uptime, response time, resolution time, and a penalty for each. (The penalty schedule was always the longest page.)

None of them said: if this system's answers become systematically wrong, this is the threshold at which we escalate. That clause did not exist in my world. It should have.

Zillow is the case that showed me the gap. Its platform stayed up, answered fast, breached nothing, and kept buying houses on a model the market had already left behind. Every dashboard I have built would have shown it green, and I would have missed it completely.

That gap is the book: Reliability in the Age of AI. It rests on four questions I call DIME (Data, Infrastructure, Model, Ethics and Trust), asked of any system that makes decisions. The cases are public: Zillow, Knight Capital, Google Flu Trends, Watson for Oncology, Amazon's hiring model. The operating lessons come from the estates I have priced and read.

I did not build AI systems. I built the reliability systems that AI is now exposing as incomplete, which is why I can see where they stop. Five chapters are drafted.

If your estate had that clause, who would own the escalation?

20 Prompts to Use AI in Microsoft Word

Follow AI Simplified for more:

------

Most founders write every important document twice.

Once in a rush.
Then again at 11pm, when it actually matters.

Proposals. Investor updates. Hiring plans.
Policies nobody wants to read.
They all start as a blank page and a blinking cursor.

And most people using AI in Word make it worse.
They type one lazy line.
They get back generic, robotic copy.
Then they spend an hour making it sound human again.

I've done exactly that.
Before, a proposal took me most of a day.
Now it takes a focused hour, and it reads better.

Same tools I had before.
Same Word document.
What changed wasn't the tool.
It was treating AI like a sharp editor, not a ghostwriter.

You stay the author.
It handles the outline, the tightening and the checking.

That's the idea behind these 20 prompts.
They work with Copilot in Word, Claude for Microsoft 365 and ChatGPT for Word.

The ones I'd start with:

— Plan and draft: a full outline with word counts before you write a line.
— Mark the gaps: it puts [ADD] wherever your own facts belong. No made-up numbers.
— Rewrite and improve: shorter sentences, active voice, same meaning.
— Change the tone: two versions, one light touch and one full rewrite.
— Cut it down: hit your word count without losing the call to action.
— Proofread: every error in a table, without touching your style.
— Get honest feedback: a 1 to 10 score from a tough but fair reader.
— Format it: headings, tables and a table of contents in one pass.
— Extract actions: every owner, deadline and decision in one table.
— Repurpose it: turn the doc into an email, an FAQ or a one-page brief.

The underrated one is prompt 16.
Compare two versions of a contract or proposal.
It lists every change in meaning.
And flags anything that could create a legal, financial or reputational risk.
That's the one I'd want before signing anything.

My advice?
Start with prompt 2 on your next proposal.
Give it your outline and notes, and let it mark every gap with [ADD].
You'll see how much faster a first draft gets when nothing is made up.

The formula behind all 20:
Role + Task + Audience + Goal + Tone + Length + Limits.

The founders moving fastest aren't writing more.
They're rewriting less.

The most significant structural shift I am observing in data engineering for 2026 is not about which tool is trending, but about the collapse of the boundary between data engineering and software engineering. The rise of "vibe coding" and autonomous AI agents that can generate and deploy entire data pipelines means that the traditional separation between writing a transformation and deploying it into production is vanishing.

The non-obvious consequence I see in production is that the scarce resource is no longer the ability to write code. It is the ability to design the operational contracts that make autonomous code safe. In 2026, the most effective data engineers are not the ones who can write the fastest Spark job or the most elegant SQL. They are the ones who can encode cost, quality, and compliance policies as machine-readable constraints that an AI agent must satisfy before it can deploy a pipeline.

Another development that is under-discussed is the emergence of the "workflow engineer" as a distinct specialization. AI is making data engineering easier to enter and larger in scope at the same time. The teams winning are not the ones with the most junior engineers using low-code tools. They are the ones who have senior engineers designing the guardrails, fallbacks, and validation gates that the junior engineers and AI agents operate within.

For recruiters and hiring managers: I am not looking for a role that asks me to write SQL or tune a pipeline. I am seeking a problem where I can design the operational constraints, validation frameworks, and fallback strategies that make autonomous data pipelines predictable and safe. If your organization is adopting AI agents for pipeline generation but struggling to enforce cost, quality, or compliance policies, I want to hear about the specific autonomy levels and governance gaps you are navigating.

What is the one policy in your current data environment that, if encoded as a machine-enforceable constraint, would enable you to safely double the number of pipelines your team can deploy per week?

“I feel my brain is slowly melting” – I heard this so many times last week!
The interference between the AI and cybersecurity industry is complex… and painful. 

On the one hand, demand for cybersecurity services grew in 2026 (12% increase as compared to 2025), at a pace similar to or slightly faster than 2025. 

In some areas, even better - cloud security posture management and threat intelligence are growing by 30% ARR now.

But hiring went the other way, sadly (dropping by 30% in a year).

Moreover, since most cybersecurity jobs are strictly technical, developers in the cybersecurity space feel the effects of the colonization of their brains by AI more than anyone.

No wonder my talk entitled “Brain Economy and Cognitive Debt: Why Human Cognition Is Becoming the Ultimate Workplace Asset” sparked interest at the prestigious OWASP® Foundation 2026 conference at the Hyatt Regency in San Francisco — my first ever cybersecurity conference, for that matter.

Indeed, when AI invades almost any area of life, and especially our work, we need to take custody of our brains – take care of our most precious tool and keep it sharp.

Besides, it was a pleasure – all geeks in the audience, plus one of the most beautiful venues I ever spoke at!

In moments like these, I feel “This is it!”

When my PhD contract in computational neuroscience expired 9 years ago, I found myself at the crossroads.

I could have chosen the path to get employed as a Data Scientist, or I could have chosen to follow my own path: take the pay of joy and just see where it leads me.

And at that fateful decision point, I chose the right path.

Today, I know that education – through science, wonder, and laughter – is my life mission.

And every day when I teach (especially with smart cookies in the audience) is a honeymoon.

Cordial thanks to Izar Tarandach, Aram H., and their team for giving me that chance to speak, and to Sam Stepanyan, Andrea Hepker, Oscar Pineda, Arkadii Yakovets, Jennifer Kent, and many others for attending.

Perhaps our paths will cross one day again!

It was also great to meet you again, Dawid Czagan :)

HERCCS - The Framework  - Friday & May initiative

Most growing companies treat HR, Employee Relations, and Corporate Costs as three separate, disconnected functions.
  - HR handles hiring and visas.
  - Admin handles office leases, insurance, and renewals.
  - Finance looks at payroll totals at the end of the month.

In a 20-to-150-person company, that separation creates silent leaks that rarely show up on a standard P&L until margins start hurting.

This is the exact gap HERCCS (HR, Employee Relations & Corporate Cost Consolidation) is built to solve.

Here’s how the HERCCS framework works, and why consolidating these functions changes how a business operates:

1. True Cost Visibility (Beyond Base Salary)
Most owners look at basic monthly payroll. They miss the 15%–25% sitting in end-of-service gratuity accrual, visa/medical pools, mobilization costs, and underutilized support capacity. HERCCS maps the true, fully-loaded Cost-to-Company against actual functional output so leaders never make blind, salary-only cuts that hurt operations.

2. Preventive Employee Relations (Stopping Disputes Before They Cost You)
In the UAE and wider GCC, one poorly handled termination, unclear contract transition, or delayed settlement can quickly turn into a DMCC/MOHRE dispute, legal fees, and management distraction. HERCCS builds audit-resistant documentation and clean exit/restructuring protocols before friction escalates.

3. Overhead & Vendor Consolidation
Small and midsize firms routinely overpay on recurring corporate overheads—commercial leases, corporate medical insurance renewals, PRO services, and fragmented software—simply because no single leader owns both the operational need and the commercial negotiation. Consolidating these under one lens typically uncovers 5%–10% in immediate annual savings.

4. Single-System Intelligence (Replacing Scattered Spreadsheets)
When headcount, leave, visa expiries, and departmental budgets live across five different Excel files, decisions are always reactive. Pairing HERCCS with an AI-enabled HRIS (One Stop Intelligence™) puts people data, compliance alerts, and monthly cash burn in one live view.

The takeaway for founders and MDs:
You don’t need a bloated corporate hierarchy to have big-company financial and people discipline. When HR, Employee Relations, and Corporate Cost Control work as one connected system, you protect your cash, protect your best people, and scale without administrative chaos.
